title: Event-driven order processing
summary: Checkout publishes one event to Kafka; payments, inventory and email each consume it at their own pace.
intro: Instead of the checkout service calling payments, inventory and email one after another, and failing if any of them is slow, it records a single fact (“order placed”) in a Kafka topic and returns. Each downstream service reads the topic with its own offset. A slow email sender falls behind without holding anyone else up, and a new service can be added later and replay the history from the start.
fits: Several teams owning separate services around shared business events

diagram.caption: Checkout appends order events to one Kafka topic. Three consumers read it independently: watch the email sender fall behind and catch up in bursts while payments keeps pace.

steps.title: Checkout records one event
steps.text: When an order is placed, checkout appends an `OrderPlaced` event, keyed by order id, to the `orders` topic and responds to the customer. It doesn’t know or care who reads it.

steps.title: Each consumer keeps its own place
steps.text: Payments, inventory and email are separate consumer groups. Kafka tracks an offset for each, so they read the same events independently and at different speeds.

steps.title: Slow consumers catch up later
steps.text: The email sender polls every couple of seconds and takes several events at once. It’s often behind, which is fine: the events wait in the topic, and nothing upstream slows down.

steps.title: Results go to each service’s own store
steps.text: Payments writes charges to its own PostgreSQL database. Services never share a database; if one needs another’s data, it reads the events or publishes its own.

good: Services are decoupled in time: one being slow or down doesn’t break checkout
Adding a consumer (fraud checks, analytics) needs no change to checkout
The topic is a replayable history, useful for rebuilding a service’s state or backfilling a new one
Keying by order id keeps each order’s events in order within a partition
watch: Consumers must be idempotent: after a crash, Kafka redelivers events since the last committed offset
Eventual consistency: right after checkout, inventory may not have reserved stock yet
Tracing one order across services needs correlation ids and good observability
Event schemas become a contract between teams; change them carefully, with a schema registry and Avro or Protobuf

swaps.text: On AWS without running Kafka: publish to SNS and fan out to one SQS queue per service, or use EventBridge rules.
If the steps must happen in order with compensation on failure (refund if stock runs out), use a workflow engine instead.
To avoid losing events when the database write succeeds but the publish fails, write to an outbox table and stream it to Kafka with change data capture.
